This paper focuses on the Energy Equivalence Rule (EER) that predicts that population energy use is invariant with average body-size. The authors have examined the EER by applying it on a large dataset including 183 soil food webs across the globe, taking into consideration the trophic position of the species under study.
The strengths of the study are:
1. The validity of the EER is a timely question and is subject of debate from theoretical as well as empirical perspectives.
2. The dataset used is unique given the number of food webs and species under study, as well as the global distribution of the food webs. The food webs are nicely comparable as they are all soil food webs.
3. The study is scientifically novel, as the application of the EER on the dataset takes into consideration aspects of food web architecture and the trophic positioning of the species.
4. Also novel is de comparison between measures of population metabolism and total energy flux.
5. The study is well carried out.
6. The results are well presented with an adequate number of clarifying figures.
7. The results are scientifically interesting and relevant, as the soil food webs seem to deviate from the EER in a principal and statistically significant manner. Expectations regarding trophic positioning (primary, secondary, predatory consumers) seem to be confirmed, although not always at the level of statistical significance.
8. The findings are well discussed but see my remarks below.
On the basis of these strengths the study qualifies to be published in a high quality scientific journal.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Ecologists have long debated the universality of the energetic equivalence rule, which posits that population energy use should be invariant with average body size due to negative size–density scaling. We explore size–density and size–energy use scaling across 183 geographically–distributed soil invertebrate food webs (comprising 55,054 individual soil invertebrates) to investigate the universality of these fundamental energetic equivalence rule assumptions across trophic levels and varying food web structure. Additionally, we compare two measures of energy use to investigate size–energy use relationships: population metabolism and energy fluxes. We find that size–density scaling does not support energetic equivalence in soil communities. Furthermore, evidence of energetic equivalence is dependent on the estimate of energy use applied, the trophic level of consumers, and food web properties. Our study demonstrates a need to integrate food web energetics and trophic structure to better understand how energetic constraints shape the body size structure of terrestrial ecosystems.

---

## Introduction

The scaling of body size with organism metabolism and abundance are underlying expectations and ecological properties on the scaling of some of the most widely observed, studied, and debated biological organism body size and population energy use estimates, despite early relationships. Yet, there is persisting discord around the generality of the energetic equivalence rule (EER) across ecosystems. This partly stems from variation in the underlying biological assumptions of the EER, differences in approaches used to estimate community body size–energy use relationships, and limited consideration of how EER scaling depends on organism trophic position and food web architecture. To date, few studies have quantified the influence of these advancements in size–density scaling to understand energetic constraints of food webs over two decades ago.

Assessing the EER is fundamentally reliant on determining the scaling relationship between population body size and energy use. The EER is a central expectation of the Metabolic Theory of Ecology (MTE), which predicts that population energy use (hereafter, En, the total energy consumption required to support population (density) n biomass) should be invariant with respect to population–average body size, that is, En ∝ Mn 0. This is based on the underlying assumptions that 1) individual organism energy use i (Ei) scales with whole–organism body size Mi with a positive ¾ (Ei ∝ Mi 0.75) exponent, and 2) the abundance (i.e., density) N of individuals scales with population body size M with a negative ¾ (N∝M–0.75) exponent. A zero exponent of body size–energy use scaling of populations in a given community (i.e., En ∝ Mn 0) should only be met if whole organism body size–energy use (i.e., Ei ∝ Mi) and size–density (N∝Mb) inverse relationships have opposite exponent values (e.g., Ei ∝ Mi 0.75 and N∝M–0.75). Numerous studies have found a –0.75 size–density scaling exponent (N∝M–0.75) among populations within communities, though many others have found this varies considerably across taxa. These observed deviations likely arise from taxonomic variation in the allometric exponent of basal metabolic rates and varying energetic constraints across trophic levels, life history traits, environmental conditions, and spatial scale. Nevertheless, an expectation of a –0.75 size–density exponent is still widely employed at both local and macro–ecological scales. Despite the fundamental assumptions of the EER, few studies have analysed both size–density and size–energy use relationships to detect energetic equivalence, and most assume energetic equivalence based only on size–density (N∝M–0.75) or whole–organism body size–energy use (Ei ∝ Mi 0.75) scaling. Furthermore, describing size–energy use scaling relationships poses the challenge of assessing population energy use, which is typically achieved by quantifying population metabolism. This approach, however, does not consider additional energetic expenditure due to the inefficiency of trophic energy transfer, losses to predation from higher trophic levels, and other trophic–level–dependent variation in energy loss. Although the EER is derived from macro–scale patterns (the GSDR), we should still expect this rule to apply for communities at carrying capacity, which would theoretically be evident from a size–density scaling relationship exponent of –0.75. Arguably, however, a more robust test of the EER at the local community scale would be to examine the population energy use–body size relationship, as this accounts for differences in energy use due to factors like taxonomic composition and trophic structure.

Size–density and size–energy use scaling relationships have been shown to vary systematically across trophic levels. While some studies have explored body size scaling relationships within a food web context, they lack further synthesis into the comparison between these size–density scaling exponents on their resulting size–energy use scaling. Energy availability decreases with increasing trophic level and body size, due to inefficient energy transfer from resources to consumers. Therefore, the scaling of size–density and size–energy use should be N∝M<–0.75 and En ∝ Mn <0, respectively, across all trophic levels, compared with N∝M–0.75 and En ∝ Mn 0 within single trophic levels that share the same energy pool. However, secondary consumers typically span multiple trophic levels that do not directly access basal resources and tend to prefer larger prey, so they should have the steepest size–density and size–energy use scaling exponents due to greater energetic constraints (although there are documented exceptions across aquatic versus terrestrial systems). Systematic deviations from expected scaling exponents related to trophic positioning of species question the theoretical foundation of the EER and call for a food web approach that discriminates among trophic levels, as information on energetic constraints could be obscured by ignoring trophic differentiation.

Whilst there has been research into environmental drivers of size–density scaling relationships underlying the EER, how variation in food web architecture and estimators of energy use affect these relationships remains unexplored (but see Loeuille & Loreau which examines how body size affects species interactions). Alternative measures of energy use, such as trophic energy flux, account for total transfer of energy in and out of a population and can therefore describe total energetic losses (and thus expenditure) due to metabolism, assimilation efficiency, and consumption by higher trophic levels (i.e., predation). These losses must be balanced by energetic gains and are therefore directly related to population energy use. Thus, despite uncertainty that is inherently introduced by modelling energy fluxes based on published input parameters, measures of total energy consumption (i.e., influx of energy into a given food web node before assimilation) should provide more precise estimates of population energy use that can be integrated into analyses of size–energy use scaling relationships in food webs.

Here we analyse size–density (N∝Mb) and size–energy use (En ∝ Mn b) scaling using a comprehensive dataset of individual body sizes (body mass in mg) in soil invertebrate food webs (i.e., local communities) across four geographic locations (i.e., 183 food webs comprising 55,054 individual invertebrates). We investigate the universality of size–density scaling relationships (based on individual size distributions as opposed to population–level size–density scaling relationships) and their likelihood of indicating energetic equivalence in soil communities of primary and secondary consumers. We compare two different estimates of energy use to investigate differences in size–energy use relationships, population metabolism (In ∝ Mn) and energy fluxes (Fn ∝ Mn), and investigate whether these scaling exponents are reflected by size–density relationships. Additionally, we investigate the marginal effects of node richness (i.e., number of nodes within each food web, where a node is defined as organism taxonomic order), trophic similarity (i.e., mean similarity between nodes per food web), and omnivory (i.e., trophic level omnivory of secondary consumers) on the deviation of food webs from predicted size–metabolism or size–energy flux exponents. We hypothesise that (1) N∝Mb and En ∝ Mn b scaling across all trophic levels (i.e., entire food webs) and for secondary consumers will be more negative than the MTE expectations of scaling exponents (i.e., N∝M<–0.75 and En ∝ Mn <0) due to attenuating trophic transfer efficiency at higher trophic levels. However, we acknowledge that increasing energetic constraints at higher trophic positions may also be partially relaxed by increasing prey richness, available energy sources, and spatial scale of movement of larger–bodied consumers. In contrast, we hypothesise that (2) primary consumers will exhibit N∝M–0.75 and En ∝ Mn 0 scaling because individuals within their trophic guilds feed from and compete over the same basal resource base. We also hypothesise that (3) En ∝ Mn b scaling using metabolism I as an estimate of energy use will be less likely to produce scaling exponents that meet expectations compared to energy flux F, as metabolism does not account for additional energetic expenditure due to assimilation (in)efficiency and losses to predation by higher trophic level consumers. Finally, we hypothesise that (4) deviations from EER expectations of En ∝ Mn 0 scaling will be smaller in food webs with higher node richness and trophic similarity due to greater resource competition imposing proportionately stronger energetic constraints on larger–bodied consumers. Conversely, we expect increasing deviations from En ∝ Mn 0 scaling with omnivory as energetic constraints may be relaxed when consumers feed across more energy sources, leading to En ∝ Mn 0 scaling exponents > 0. However, we also assume these effects of food web properties on deviations from EER expectations will vary across trophic levels due to differences discussed above.

---

## Results

Testing the energetic equivalence rule without trophic differentiation
Scaling exponents of soil invertebrate consumers across all trophic levels in soil food webs were, on average, more positive than expected for size–density (i.e., N∝M>–0.75, mean=–0.174, median=–0.152, σ2=0.05), size–metabolism (i.e., In ∝ Mn >0, mean=0.134, median = 0.164, σ2=0.07), and size–energy flux (i.e., Fn ∝ Mn >0, mean=0.204, median=0.195, σ2=0.09) relationships. Nevertheless, scaling exponents derived from both measures of energy use (In ∝ Mn and Fn ∝ Mn) appeared to have a similar central tendency (kurtosis=4, and In ∝ Mn σ2=0.07, Fn ∝ Mn σ2=0.09) around values expected by the MTE, within the confidence interval of exponent estimates. At the whole food web level, metabolism as an estimate of energy use appeared to better fit EER expectations compared to energy flux, as 50.3% of all soil food webs met scaling expectations for size–metabolism relationships compared to 41.5% for size–energy flux relationships. There was a significant positive and negative effect of node richness on the deviation of food webs from the hypothesised size–metabolism and size–energy flux exponent (p<0.01), respectively. We also found a significant negative effect of trophic similarity (i.e., the mean similarity among all nodes in the trophic level (primary consumers or predators) on the deviation of whole food webs from both the hypothesised size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn 0) and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn 0) exponents (p<0.01).

Variation in energetic scaling patterns across trophic levels and food web structure
Similar to the trends in EER scaling relationships observed for whole food webs, primary consumers produced scaling exponents that were, on average, more positive than expected for size–density (N∝M>–0.75, mean=–0.191, median=–0.109, σ2=0.16), size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn >0, mean=0.261, median=0.268, σ2=0.12), and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn >0 mean = 0.761, median = 0.646, σ2=0.51) relationships. Secondary consumer scaling exponents were, on average, more positive than expected for size–density (N∝M>–0.75, mean=–0.218, median = –0.201, σ2=0.06) relationships. However, as we predicted, they were more negative for size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn <0, mean=–0.039, median=–0.003, σ2=0.14) and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn <0, mean=–0.394, median = –0.524, σ2=0.57) relationships. Out of 173 primary consumer communities, 1.1% met scaling expectations for size–density (N∝M–0.75), 42.9% met size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn 0) expectations, and 46.3% met size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn 0) scaling expectations of the MTE. Comparatively, out of 180 secondary consumer communities, 2.8% met scaling expectations for size–density, 41.4% met size–metabolism scaling expectations, and 54.1% met size–energy flux scaling expectations of the MTE. We also found less variation (i.e., higher kurtosis and variance of the respective density functions for scaling exponent estimates) around the mean and median exponents for the scaling of body size with energy fluxes (Fn ∝ Mn) compared to metabolism (In ∝ Mn) for secondary consumers, though the opposite was true for primary consumer kurtosis values. These observed differences between measures of energy use were further corroborated by significant differences in the probability distributions of estimated metabolism versus energy flux exponents for both primary (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test D=0.411, p<0.01) and secondary consumers (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test D=0.406, p<0.01). Contrary to our hypothesis, we found that mean and median exponent values for In ∝ Mn and Fn ∝ Mn relationships were closer to zero for secondary consumers than for primary consumers. To ensure that our results were not notably biased by differences among datasets in the measurement of environmental temperature, we calculated metabolic rates and energy fluxes with temperatures extracted from WorldClim and re–ran analyses to test for the sensitivity of EER scaling results to variations in environmental temperature, which yielded no qualitative changes in our results.

We only found a significant positive effect of trophic similarity within secondary consumer food webs on the deviation from size–metabolism scaling expectations (In ∝ Mn 0). In contrast, for size–energy use scaling based on energy fluxes, we found a significant positive effect of node richness and negative effects of trophic similarity and omnivory on the deviation from size–energy flux scaling expectations for secondary consumers (Fn ∝ Mn 0, p<0.01). However, we found no significant effects of node richness or trophic similarity on deviations from the size–metabolism or size–energy flux exponents expected by the EER for primary consumers (p<0.05).

## Methods

Soilinvertebratecommunitysampling
Soilinvertebratecommunitydatawascollectedfromfourlocations(AotearoaNewZealand,Indonesia,Canada,andU.S.A)throughsamplingeffortsofthreelarge–scaleprojects. (1) The Aotearoa New Zealand plots (People Cities & Nature programme) were established in forest patches within nine cities spanning ~9o of latitude. These were part of a 60–year–old planted and primary old–growth urban forest chronosequence (n=73). (2) The Indonesian (EFForTS project) study plots (n=30) were established in remnant tropical rainforest, jungle rubber agroforest systems, rubber monocultures, and oil palm monocultures across two landscapes surrounding Bukit Duabelas and Harapan rainforest reserves in the Jambi Province, Sumatra, Indonesia. The ECOWORM project study plots (n=80) in (3) the United States (St John’s forest, Minnesota) and (4) Canada (Barrier Lake North, Barrier Lake South, and Bull Creek Hills in the Canadian Rocky Mountains, Kananaskis Valley, Alberta) were established in maple and aspen forest sites, respectively, whereby each of these forests contained a low–invasion and a high–invasion exotic earthworm area–per forest (10 plots in low– and 10 plots in high–invasion areas).

Soilinvertebratecommunitydatacollectionandpreparation
Aotearoa New Zealand soil invertebrates were sampled between November 2019–February 2020 (austral summer) from three 50 × 50 cm subplots by taking one macrofauna soil core (22 cm diameter, 10 cm deep from the mineral soil layers) and one mesofauna soil core (5 cm diameter, 10 cm deep mineral soil layers) per subplot. Macro– and mesofauna were extracted from the soil cores using heat extraction and identified in the laboratory to family or order level (i.e., node). Individual body length (mm) was converted to fresh body size (mg) using length–size scaling relationships according to different invertebrate phylogenetic groups from published literature. Soil invertebrate collection from all other geographic regions followed similar procedures, whereby mesofauna were collected either from small cores (5 cm diameter, 10 cm deep) or 16×16 cm quadrats (5 cm deep), and macrofauna were collected from large soil cores (20 cm diameter, 10 cm deep), leaf litter sieving (0.5 m2 ECOWORM and 1 m2 EFFForTS), and mustard extraction for earthworms (0.25 m2). Invertebrate body size ranged from 4.82×10–5 mg – 5290 mg. For more detailed methods see Antunes.

To analyse size–energy use relationships, we took a size–binning (rather than populations of competing organisms) approach by taking the natural logarithm of all body sizes, across all taxonomic groups, and grouped them into 0.25 ln(mg) size class bins (following Reuman). This size binning approach was used for two reasons. Firstly, population-level information (i.e., species level taxonomic resolution) was not always available for our data, though individual body sizes were. Secondly, these methods have both yielded similar size–density scaling relationships within many food webs studied, so we can assume this consistency also applies to tests of size–energy use scaling relationships. We took the median of the natural logarithm of body size of each size class bin per plot, across all taxonomic groups. Abundance was then calculated as the number of individuals in each size class bin (and per node type for analysing within trophic levels) per plot and scaled to 1 m2. For analysing size–density relationships, the counts of soil invertebrate fresh body sizes (mg) across and within trophic levels were scaled up to 1 m2. We calculated individual metabolic rates I (J hr–1) for invertebrates within each taxonomic group (see Table S3 for regressions applied to each taxon) using the following equation from Ehnes et al.

I=exp(ln(io)+α×ln(M)−E/(k×T)) (1)

Where k is Boltzmann’s constant (8.62×10–5), T is environmental temperature in Kelvin, E the activation energy, io the taxa specific normalisation constant and, α is the allometric exponent. Plot–level mean soil temperature from a three–month period preceding soil sampling was collected using data loggers for the Aotearoa New Zealand. Local area–level annual soil temperature (over a one year period) for the ECOWORM plots was collected from online weather databases (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration n.d.). Plot–level mean soil temperature was collected over a 2.5 month period using data loggers for the EFFForTS data. We took the natural logarithm of individual invertebrate metabolic rates, summed per size class bin per plot, and scaled to 1 m2.

Foodwebreconstructionandconsumerenergyintakecalculation
To reconstruct soil food webs, nodes were defined according to organism taxonomic order (or family level for Hymenoptera and Coleoptera) for which information on their general feeding preferences was obtained. We constructed a meta–matrix of binary consumer–resource interactions, where feeding links were assigned based on feeding preferences obtained from literature. Energy influx in J day–1 into each consumer node within a local food web (i.e., plot) was calculated using the food–web energetics approach as described by Barnes and Gauzens to quantify the energy intake of organisms across the 183 local food webs. To calculate energy fluxes, we assumed that losses in energy from consumer nodes (via metabolism and predation) were balanced by intake of energy through resource consumption. Energy flux values were calculated taking into account the assimilation efficiency of energy by consumers based on the resources they feed on (i.e., primary versus secondary consumers).

Using the fluxing function from the fluxweb package in R, the influx of energy to consumer (j) was calculated as:

Σi(Wij×eij×Fij)=Ij+Σj(Wij×Fj) (2)

where eij is the assimilation efficiency by which a consumer (j) converts energy consumed from its resource (i) into energy for metabolism and biomass production. To determine the assimilation efficiency of energy by consumers based on the resources they feed on, eij was set to 0.906 for animals (e.g., as resources of predators), 0.545 for plants, 0.158 for detritus, 0.6 for bacteria, and 0.5 for fungi. Metabolic rate Ij for all animal consumers was equal to the summed individual metabolic rates per node, per plot. Ij was set to 1 for all basal resources (bacteria, detritus, plants, and fungi). Fij=Wij×Fj is the flux of energy to a consumer where Fj is the sum of fluxes into a node and Wij is the proportion of Fj obtained by the node according to scaled consumer preferences (wij) to the biomasses of different available prey as:

Wij=wij×Bi / Σj×wij×Bj (3)

where Bi and Bj are the resource and consumer biomasses, respectively. Bi for all animal resources and Bj for all animal consumers were equal to the summed fresh body masses (mg) of all individuals per node type, per plot. All basal resource biomasses were set to be equal to the average biomass of all consumer node types per plot to set near–equal preferences of omnivores between predatory links and basal resources. This was done to reduce extreme preferences of omnivores towards basal resources, such as plants and detritus that typically have much higher biomasses compared to soil invertebrate prey, but are less preferred by them as they are lower in nutritional value. Studies have tested whether the assignment of feeding preferences of omnivores between basal resources (in this case, just plants) and animals could affect energy fluxes by altering feeding preferences for plants between 0.2 to 0.9 and found no significant change in the outcome of their analysis; therefore, we set equal preferences between basal resources and animal prey in our food webs. Additionally, to reduce the amount of energy predators consume from their own biomass pool and unrealistic feeding preferences toward cannibalism, we set the feeding preferences of any cannibalistic links to 0.1.

Because body size was grouped into size class bins (irrespective of food web node) per plot to analyse size–energy relationships and energy flux was calculated per food web node per plot (Fnode), to attribute the proportion of ingoing energy flux from each food web node to each size class bin per plot (Fsizeclass), we calculated proportional energy flux according to the summed metabolism of each size class (Isizeclass) and energy intake of that node as:

Fsizeclass= f(Isizeclass,node =Inode)×Fnode (4)

Where Inode represents the total metabolism of a node. Energy fluxes were then natural logarithm–transformed and scaled to 1 m2.

To obtain food web metrics that could explain variation in expectations of size–density scaling and energetic equivalence of soil food webs, we quantified mean trophic similarity among nodes (for the whole food web, and within primary and secondary consumers) by calculating the average Jaccard similarity among consumer nodes based on their feeding links with resource nodes. Specifically, trophic similarity TSij between consumer i and j represents the similarity in their diets, estimated with a Jaccard index:

TSij=|Pi∩Pj|/|Pi∪Pj| (5)

Pi represents the set of prey of consumer i and |Pi ∩ Pj| is the cardinality of the intersection of Pi and Pj (i.e., the number of prey common to consumer i and j). High trophic similarity indicates a large average overlap among consumers, which can occur in the absence of omnivory, e.g. if many specialists feed on a shared resource. We calculated observed node richness as the number of nodes within each food web (total nodes in the food web, and the number of primary and secondary consumer nodes). Furthermore, we calculated trophic level omnivory of secondary consumer i (Oi) as the variance of the trophic levels of its prey:

Oi=1/ni Σj=1...ni(TLj−TLx̄i)2 (6)

Where TLx̄i is the average trophic level of the prey of species i. For each local food web, we further determined the prey–averaged trophic level (TLi) of each node, such that the trophic level was equal to one for basal resources, two for primary consumers, and >2 for secondary consumers as:

TLi=1/ni Σj=1...niTLj (7)

Where ni is the number of prey of species i, and j are prey of species i.

Statisticalanalysis
To analyse size–density relationships (N∝Mb) across whole soil invertebrate food webs and within primary and secondary consumers, we used maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to estimate the exponent b (i.e., λ+1) derived from individual size distributions (ISD) of all individual body sizes (scaled to 1 m2) within soil invertebrate communities using the sizeSpectra package in R. To check the fit of models against observed body size data (x), rank–frequency plots were produced giving the natural logarithm–rank of the number of observations ≥x against the value of x.

To analyse size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn), and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn) scaling relationships across whole soil invertebrate food webs and within primary and secondary consumers, we used ordinary least squared (OLS) regression using logarithm median body mass data (scaled to 1 m2). MLE and OLS regression models were run across all communities (i.e., plots) within the four geographic regions. The 95% confidence intervals around the exponent values were also calculated, and exponents were considered to meet N∝M–0.75, In ∝ Mn 0, or Fn ∝ Mn 0 expectations if these confidence intervals included the expected exponent value. We excluded all resulting models with less than 10 body size class bins or individuals per food web from our analysis due to insufficient data for estimating reliable model fits. To evaluate the distribution of scaling exponents around the mean and median values of our models, we calculated the kurtosis of their probability density functions using the kurtosis function in R. In this regard, higher kurtosis values indicate greater deviation from a normal distribution, reflecting increased variation around the mean and median exponent values. We also ran a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, to determine if our two sample distributions (e.g., metabolism and energy flux exponents) come from the same probability distribution using the ks.test function in R. To analyse size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn), and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn) scaling relationships across whole soil invertebrate food webs and within primary and secondary consumers, we also used ranged major axis (RMA) regression using the lmodel2 package in R to analyse these relationships. RMA regression is used when both x and y variables (e.g., median body size, abundance, metabolism, and energy flux) in the regression equation are random. RMA regression models were run across all communities (i.e., plots) within the four geographic regions. We excluded all resulting models with less than 10 body size class bins or individuals per food web from our analysis due to insufficient data for estimating reliable model fits. As a result, our analyses yielded a total of 183 food webs (i.e., comprising both primary and secondary consumers) and 360 trophic level models (180 models for primary consumers and 180 for secondary consumer food webs). Our analyses yielded a total of 183 food webs (i.e., comprising both primary and secondary consumers) and 355 trophic level models (173 models for primary consumers and 179 for secondary consumer food webs).

Additionally, we investigated whether the likelihood of size–density and size–energy use relationships to meet EER expectations could be explained by variation in food web structure. To do so, for all food webs, we constructed a normal linear model testing for the response of the absolute logarithm–deviation of observed exponents from expected size–energy use exponents (In ∝ Mn 0 and Fn ∝ Mn 0) to omnivory, node richness, and trophic similarity per food web and per trophic level (i.e., primary and secondary consumers). This produced six linear models in total. All statistical analyses were performed in R version R 4.4.0.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
General comments:
This thoughtful study uses a huge dataset to show that population energy use in soil
invertebrate communities does not follow the energy equivalence principle (EEP), and that
the scaling of energy use and population abundance does not follow the 3/4-power law, both
considered by some to be major rules of nature. Other studies have also shown energy
inequivalence for some ecological communities, but the present study is notable because it
is verified by using two different measures of energy use and by showing significant effects
of food-web structure. This study also clearly shows that one cannot reliably test the EEP by
merely examining size-abundance patterns in communities. The authors further recommend
that energy flux measurements may be more useful than measurements of metabolic rate in
testing the EEP.
We thank you for your positive and constructive thoughts and suggestions on our
manuscript. We have made every effort to address your points, as shown in our responses
below.
However, I have three major concerns that I believe that the authors should address.
(1) There seems to be a disconnect between the author’s model (Figure 1) and their
collected data on body-size distribution (Figure 2). Their model assumes that secondary
consumers have larger body sizes than primary consumers, on average, but their data show
no obvious overall difference between these trophic levels.
Response: Thank you for bringing this point to our attention. We have now bridged this
disconnect between Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 by redrawing the hypothetical scaling relationships
expected across primary and secondary consumers. Specifically, our original hypotheses
were based on general ecological theory (irrespective of ecosystem type) that assumes
predators are, on average, larger than their prey. While this is often the case in belowground
ecosystems, soil food webs also contain many primary consumer 'trophic whales' that reach
exceptionally large body sizes (e.g. earthworms and some millipedes), though the majority of
primary consumers are still very small. Predators on the other hand, are usually larger than
their prey, but there are also few (or even none) that eat large–bodied detritivores. Thus, a
more appropriate expectation of body size structure for soil food webs would be that the
upper body size range of primary and secondary consumers are similar, while the lower
range for primary consumers extends beyond that of secondary consumers (as now shown
in Fig. 1).This revised expectation now better describes the typical body size structure of soil
food webs, but without altering the overarching hypotheses and interpretation of findings in
our study related to the EER.
(2) The authors claim that their study is the first to compare size-abundance relationships
between trophic levels, but this was done previously for aquatic macroinvertebrates, which
interestingly like the present study, also show little difference in mean body size between
primary and secondary consumers (Gjoni & Glazier 2020). However, to my knowledge, the
present study is the first that directly tests the EEP at different trophic levels.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that our study is the first to directly investigate the
EER across multiple trophic levels within a food web context, and to also compare different
measures of energy use. We believe this novel approach addresses a critical gap in the
current literature. We have carefully revised our novelty statements throughout the
manuscript to this effect.
(3) I am concerned about whether the authors considered that primary and secondary
consumers tend to have different assimilation efficiencies, which may affect their estimates
of energy fluxes based only on energy consumption rate. This should be clarified.
Response: We apologise for the lack of clarity on this key aspect. We have indeed
accounted for differing assimilation efficiencies across trophic levels, as well as scaling
organism efficiency with environmental temperature (sensu Lang et al. 2017 Oikos; see
supplementary information). We have added an additional sentence into the Methods
section (see lines 437-441) to improve clarity. Additionally, for a more comprehensive
methodology please refer to the “Food web reconstruction” section in the supplementary
information.
Specific comments:
1. L 103-108: Note that references 9 &10 focus on the scaling of metabolic rate, not
population abundance. Note also that reference 10 describes several intrinsic and
extrinsic factors that affect the metabolic scaling exponent.
Response: References removed.
2. L 108-109: Reference 1 shows that across life the metabolic scaling exponent is
nearer to 1 than 0.75.
Response: Reference removed.
3. L 127-131: Note that the original analysis by Damuth (1981) focused on herbivorous
mammals (primary consumers) only, thus controlling trophic level.
Response: We appreciate the point that Damuth (1981), as an example, did in fact
control for cross-trophic level variation in EER scaling. However, this study did not
discriminate between trophic levels or describe differences in scaling relationships
expected due to varying energetic constraints across trophic levels, which is what we
address in our present study.
4. L 132-134, 324-325: See also the work of Gjoni and her colleagues (e.g., Gjoni et al.
2017, 2022, 2023; Gjoni & Glazier, 2020). Gjoni & Glazier (2020) have shown that
size-abundance relationships for macroinvertebrate communities vary with trophic
level in brackish lagoons. However, the major difference between predators and prey
is the elevation of the scaling relationship, and not the slope.
Response: These suggested studies have been added, where relevant, to the
manuscript. Thank you for bringing these to our attention.
5. L 139-140: Using energy input (consumption) before assimilation may be an
unreliable method of estimating population energy use, especially if assimilation
efficiency is low and variable. Note that assimilation efficiency tends to be much
higher for animal (secondary) versus plant (primary) consumers. Please clarify.
Reponse: We took much care in accounting for assimilation efficiency in energy
intake calculations. Please see section “Food web reconstruction and consumer
energy flux calculation” within the supplementary information. Energy intake before
assimilation quantifies total resource consumption, taking into account the different
energetic demands of consumers due to different assimilation efficiencies of
organisms at different trophic levels. If we were to rather use energy intake after
assimilation, this would not account for the proportionately greater consumption rates
of lower trophic level organisms (e.g. detritivores) needed to balance their energetic
demands, as compared to predators that have relatively high assimilation
efficiencies. Therefore, we calculate energy intake per population by scaling
consumption rates according to varying assimilation efficiencies among trophic
levels. This is necessary because energetic equivalence will depend on competition
among consumers for resources based on total rates of exploitation of those
resources, rather than the proportion of energy that is eventually assimilated by
consumers. 
6. L 153-156: If energy consumption is known at each trophic level, then I suspect that

trophic-level specific assimilation efficiencies in our energy intake calculations. To do
so, energy fluxes are scaled up proportionately to the efficiency of the given energy
transfer from resource to consumer. See supplementary information for details.

consumers of all sizes in a uniform way, thus causing a change in the scaling
elevation rather than the scaling slope (as observed for size-abundance relationships

secondary consumers are expected to be larger on average than primary consumers,
as shown in Figure 1a? If so, this need not be true, as observed on brackish water
macroinvertebrate communities (Gjoni and Glazier 2020). Please clarify.
Response: A change in slope is expected due to the proportionately increasing
energetic demand with body size for secondary versus primary consumers because
of the greater energetic constraints faced by secondary consumers. We believe this
is well covered and already discussed in multiple areas throughout the introduction
(first stated in lines 126-127, 134-138) and discussion. However, we have done our
best to elaborate where possible throughout the manuscript.
8. L 301-305: Similar trophic level patterns have been shown by Gjoni and Glazier
(2020).
Response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have now cited this interesting study.
9. L 318: Change “are” to “is”.
Response: Changed.
10. L 387-415: What was the body-size range of the invertebrates collected. Which taxa
were included? Were any taxa that were present not included because they were too
small or for other reasons?
Response: See lines 400 for body size range. Please see supplementary information
for taxa included in our analyses e.g., Table S2, S3. As well as the “Statistical
analysis” section for exclusion/inclusion criteria.
11. L 415: Change “Ehnes” to “Ehnes et al.”?
Response: Fixed
12. L 437: Was assimilation efficiency adjusted to trophic level? Primary consumers tend
to have lower assimilation efficiencies than secondary consumers.
Response: Yes, trophic-level specific assimilation efficiency is a key parameter
included in energy flux calculations. Please see section “Food web reconstruction
and consumer energy flux calculation” within the supplementary information.
13. L 450: Change “supplementary for full methods” to “supplementary information for full
methods”.
Response: Changed
14. L 495-505: Why are scaling slopes predicted to be more negative for secondary
consumers? This need not be so (see e.g., Gjoni & Glazier 2020).
Response: Based on the broader literature, we hypothesised that secondary
consumers should have the steepest exponents due to increasing energetic
constraints at higher trophic levels. This expectation is covered on lines 129-138,
although we now acknowledge there are documented exceptions, as found in Gjoni &

and size–energy use scaling exponents were more negative for secondary
consumers (see Fig. 5).
15. L 507-510: On the X-axis, shouldn’t “body size” be “body mass”? Also is it dry or wet
body mass?
Response: We used estimates of live, fresh body size (mg) (synonymous with ‘wet
body mass’; see lines 392-394). More generally, we use body size throughout the
manuscript, but have now clearly defined this on line 156.

## Paper

## Abstract

Ecologists have long debated the universality of the energetic equivalence rule, which posits that population energy use should be invariant with average body size due to negative size–density scaling. We explore size–density and size–energy use scaling across 183 geographically–distributed soil invertebrate food webs (comprising 55,054 individual soil invertebrates) to investigate the universality of these fundamental energetic equivalence rule assumptions across trophic levels and varying food web structure. Additionally, we compare two measures of energy use to investigate size–energy use relationships: population metabolism and energy fluxes. We find that size–density scaling does not support energetic equivalence in soil communities. Furthermore, evidence of energetic equivalence is dependent on the estimate of energy use applied, the trophic level of consumers, and food web properties. Our study demonstrates a need to integrate food web energetics and trophic structure to better understand how energetic constraints shape the body size structure of terrestrial ecosystems.

## Introduction

The scaling of body size with organism metabolism and abundance are underlying expectations and ecological properties on the scaling of some of the most widely observed, studied, and debated biological organism body size and population energy use estimates, despite early relationships. Yet, there is persisting discord around the generality of the energetic equivalence rule (EER) across ecosystems. This partly stems from variation in the underlying biological assumptions of the EER, differences in approaches used to estimate community body size–energy use relationships, and limited consideration of how EER scaling depends on organism trophic position and food web architecture. To date, few studies have quantified the influence of these advancements in size–density scaling to understand energetic constraints of food webs over two decades ago.

Assessing the EER is fundamentally reliant on determining the scaling relationship between population body size and energy use. The EER is a central expectation of the Metabolic Theory of Ecology (MTE), which predicts that population energy use (hereafter, En, the total energy consumption required to support population (density) n biomass) should be invariant with respect to population–average body size, that is, En ∝ Mn 0. This is based on the underlying assumptions that 1) individual organism energy use i (Ei) scales with whole–organism body size Mi with a positive ¾ (Ei ∝ Mi 0.75) exponent, and 2) the abundance (i.e., density) N of individuals scales with population body size M with a negative ¾ (N∝M–0.75) exponent. A zero exponent of body size–energy use scaling of populations in a given community (i.e., En ∝ Mn 0) should only be met if whole organism body size–energy use (i.e., Ei ∝ Mi) and size–density (N∝Mb) inverse relationships have opposite exponent values (e.g., Ei ∝ Mi 0.75 and N∝M–0.75). Numerous studies have found a –0.75 size–density scaling exponent (N∝M–0.75) among populations within communities, though many others have found this varies considerably across taxa. These observed deviations likely arise from taxonomic variation in the allometric exponent of basal metabolic rates and varying energetic constraints across trophic levels, life history traits, environmental conditions, and spatial scale. Nevertheless, an expectation of a –0.75 size–density exponent is still widely employed at both local and macro–ecological scales. Despite the fundamental assumptions of the EER, few studies have analysed both size–density and size–energy use relationships to detect energetic equivalence, and most assume energetic equivalence based only on size–density (N∝M–0.75) or whole–organism body size–energy use (Ei ∝ Mi 0.75) scaling. Furthermore, describing size–energy use scaling relationships poses the challenge of assessing population energy use, which is typically achieved by quantifying population metabolism. This approach, however, does not consider additional energetic expenditure due to the inefficiency of trophic energy transfer, losses to predation from higher trophic levels, and other trophic–level–dependent variation in energy loss. Although the EER is derived from macro–scale patterns (the GSDR), we should still expect this rule to apply for communities at carrying capacity, which would theoretically be evident from a size–density scaling relationship exponent of –0.75. Arguably, however, a more robust test of the EER at the local community scale would be to examine the population energy use–body size relationship, as this accounts for differences in energy use due to factors like taxonomic composition and trophic structure.

Size–density and size–energy use scaling relationships have been shown to vary systematically across trophic levels. While some studies have explored body size scaling relationships within a food web context, they lack further synthesis into the comparison between these size–density scaling exponents on their resulting size–energy use scaling. Energy availability decreases with increasing trophic level and body size, due to inefficient energy transfer from resources to consumers. Therefore, the scaling of size–density and size–energy use should be N∝M<–0.75 and En ∝ Mn <0, respectively, across all trophic levels, compared with N∝M–0.75 and En ∝ Mn 0 within single trophic levels that share the same energy pool. However, secondary consumers typically span multiple trophic levels that do not directly access basal resources and tend to prefer larger prey, so they should have the steepest size–density and size–energy use scaling exponents due to greater energetic constraints (although there are documented exceptions across aquatic versus terrestrial systems). Systematic deviations from expected scaling exponents related to trophic positioning of species question the theoretical foundation of the EER and call for a food web approach that discriminates among trophic levels, as information on energetic constraints could be obscured by ignoring trophic differentiation.

Whilst there has been research into environmental drivers of size–density scaling relationships underlying the EER, how variation in food web architecture and estimators of energy use affect these relationships remains unexplored (but see Loeuille & Loreau which examines how body size affects species interactions). Alternative measures of energy use, such as trophic energy flux, account for total transfer of energy in and out of a population and can therefore describe total energetic losses (and thus expenditure) due to metabolism, assimilation efficiency, and consumption by higher trophic levels (i.e., predation). These losses must be balanced by energetic gains and are therefore directly related to population energy use. Thus, despite uncertainty that is inherently introduced by modelling energy fluxes based on published input parameters, measures of total energy consumption (i.e., influx of energy into a given food web node before assimilation) should provide more precise estimates of population energy use that can be integrated into analyses of size–energy use scaling relationships in food webs.

Here we analyse size–density (N∝Mb) and size–energy use (En ∝ Mn b) scaling using a comprehensive dataset of individual body sizes (body mass in mg) in soil invertebrate food webs (i.e., local communities) across four geographic locations (i.e., 183 food webs comprising 55,054 individual invertebrates). We investigate the universality of size–density scaling relationships (based on individual size distributions as opposed to population–level size–density scaling relationships) and their likelihood of indicating energetic equivalence in soil communities of primary and secondary consumers. We compare two different estimates of energy use to investigate differences in size–energy use relationships, population metabolism (In ∝ Mn) and energy fluxes (Fn ∝ Mn), and investigate whether these scaling exponents are reflected by size–density relationships. Additionally, we investigate the marginal effects of node richness (i.e., number of nodes within each food web, where a node is defined as organism taxonomic order), trophic similarity (i.e., mean similarity between nodes per food web), and omnivory (i.e., trophic level omnivory of secondary consumers) on the deviation of food webs from predicted size–metabolism or size–energy flux exponents. We hypothesise that (1) N∝Mb and En ∝ Mn b scaling across all trophic levels (i.e., entire food webs) and for secondary consumers will be more negative than the MTE expectations of scaling exponents (i.e., N∝M<–0.75 and En ∝ Mn <0) due to attenuating trophic transfer efficiency at higher trophic levels. However, we acknowledge that increasing energetic constraints at higher trophic positions may also be partially relaxed by increasing prey richness, available energy sources, and spatial scale of movement of larger–bodied consumers. In contrast, we hypothesise that (2) primary consumers will exhibit N∝M–0.75 and En ∝ Mn 0 scaling because individuals within their trophic guilds feed from and compete over the same basal resource base. We also hypothesise that (3) En ∝ Mn b scaling using metabolism I as an estimate of energy use will be less likely to produce scaling exponents that meet expectations compared to energy flux F, as metabolism does not account for additional energetic expenditure due to assimilation (in)efficiency and losses to predation by higher trophic level consumers. Finally, we hypothesise that (4) deviations from EER expectations of En ∝ Mn 0 scaling will be smaller in food webs with higher node richness and trophic similarity due to greater resource competition imposing proportionately stronger energetic constraints on larger–bodied consumers. Conversely, we expect increasing deviations from En ∝ Mn 0 scaling with omnivory as energetic constraints may be relaxed when consumers feed across more energy sources, leading to En ∝ Mn 0 scaling exponents > 0. However, we also assume these effects of food web properties on deviations from EER expectations will vary across trophic levels due to differences discussed above.

## Results

Testing the energetic equivalence rule without trophic differentiation
Scaling exponents of soil invertebrate consumers across all trophic levels in soil food webs were, on average, more positive than expected for size–density (i.e., N∝M>–0.75, mean=–0.174, median=–0.152, σ2=0.05), size–metabolism (i.e., In ∝ Mn >0, mean=0.134, median = 0.164, σ2=0.07), and size–energy flux (i.e., Fn ∝ Mn >0, mean=0.204, median=0.195, σ2=0.09) relationships. Nevertheless, scaling exponents derived from both measures of energy use (In ∝ Mn and Fn ∝ Mn) appeared to have a similar central tendency (kurtosis=4, and In ∝ Mn σ2=0.07, Fn ∝ Mn σ2=0.09) around values expected by the MTE, within the confidence interval of exponent estimates. At the whole food web level, metabolism as an estimate of energy use appeared to better fit EER expectations compared to energy flux, as 50.3% of all soil food webs met scaling expectations for size–metabolism relationships compared to 41.5% for size–energy flux relationships. There was a significant positive and negative effect of node richness on the deviation of food webs from the hypothesised size–metabolism and size–energy flux exponent (p<0.01), respectively. We also found a significant negative effect of trophic similarity (i.e., the mean similarity among all nodes in the trophic level (primary consumers or predators) on the deviation of whole food webs from both the hypothesised size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn 0) and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn 0) exponents (p<0.01).

Variation in energetic scaling patterns across trophic levels and food web structure
Similar to the trends in EER scaling relationships observed for whole food webs, primary consumers produced scaling exponents that were, on average, more positive than expected for size–density (N∝M>–0.75, mean=–0.191, median=–0.109, σ2=0.16), size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn >0, mean=0.261, median=0.268, σ2=0.12), and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn >0 mean = 0.761, median = 0.646, σ2=0.51) relationships. Secondary consumer scaling exponents were, on average, more positive than expected for size–density (N∝M>–0.75, mean=–0.218, median = –0.201, σ2=0.06) relationships. However, as we predicted, they were more negative for size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn <0, mean=–0.039, median=–0.003, σ2=0.14) and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn <0, mean=–0.394, median = –0.524, σ2=0.57) relationships. Out of 173 primary consumer communities, 1.1% met scaling expectations for size–density (N∝M–0.75), 42.9% met size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn 0) expectations, and 46.3% met size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn 0) scaling expectations of the MTE. Comparatively, out of 180 secondary consumer communities, 2.8% met scaling expectations for size–density, 41.4% met size–metabolism scaling expectations, and 54.1% met size–energy flux scaling expectations of the MTE. We also found less variation (i.e., higher kurtosis and variance of the respective density functions for scaling exponent estimates) around the mean and median exponents for the scaling of body size with energy fluxes (Fn ∝ Mn) compared to metabolism (In ∝ Mn) for secondary consumers, though the opposite was true for primary consumer kurtosis values. These observed differences between measures of energy use were further corroborated by significant differences in the probability distributions of estimated metabolism versus energy flux exponents for both primary (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test D=0.411, p<0.01) and secondary consumers (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test D=0.406, p<0.01). Contrary to our hypothesis, we found that mean and median exponent values for In ∝ Mn and Fn ∝ Mn relationships were closer to zero for secondary consumers than for primary consumers. To ensure that our results were not notably biased by differences among datasets in the measurement of environmental temperature, we calculated metabolic rates and energy fluxes with temperatures extracted from WorldClim and re–ran analyses to test for the sensitivity of EER scaling results to variations in environmental temperature, which yielded no qualitative changes in our results.

We only found a significant positive effect of trophic similarity within secondary consumer food webs on the deviation from size–metabolism scaling expectations (In ∝ Mn 0). In contrast, for size–energy use scaling based on energy fluxes, we found a significant positive effect of node richness and negative effects of trophic similarity and omnivory on the deviation from size–energy flux scaling expectations for secondary consumers (Fn ∝ Mn 0, p<0.01). However, we found no significant effects of node richness or trophic similarity on deviations from the size–metabolism or size–energy flux exponents expected by the EER for primary consumers (p<0.05).

## Methods

Soilinvertebratecommunitysampling
Soilinvertebratecommunitydatawascollectedfromfourlocations(AotearoaNewZealand,Indonesia,Canada,andU.S.A)throughsamplingeffortsofthreelarge–scaleprojects. (1) The Aotearoa New Zealand plots (People Cities & Nature programme) were established in forest patches within nine cities spanning ~9o of latitude. These were part of a 60–year–old planted and primary old–growth urban forest chronosequence (n=73). (2) The Indonesian (EFForTS project) study plots (n=30) were established in remnant tropical rainforest, jungle rubber agroforest systems, rubber monocultures, and oil palm monocultures across two landscapes surrounding Bukit Duabelas and Harapan rainforest reserves in the Jambi Province, Sumatra, Indonesia. The ECOWORM project study plots (n=80) in (3) the United States (St John’s forest, Minnesota) and (4) Canada (Barrier Lake North, Barrier Lake South, and Bull Creek Hills in the Canadian Rocky Mountains, Kananaskis Valley, Alberta) were established in maple and aspen forest sites, respectively, whereby each of these forests contained a low–invasion and a high–invasion exotic earthworm area–per forest (10 plots in low– and 10 plots in high–invasion areas).

Soilinvertebratecommunitydatacollectionandpreparation
Aotearoa New Zealand soil invertebrates were sampled between November 2019–February 2020 (austral summer) from three 50 × 50 cm subplots by taking one macrofauna soil core (22 cm diameter, 10 cm deep from the mineral soil layers) and one mesofauna soil core (5 cm diameter, 10 cm deep mineral soil layers) per subplot. Macro– and mesofauna were extracted from the soil cores using heat extraction and identified in the laboratory to family or order level (i.e., node). Individual body length (mm) was converted to fresh body size (mg) using length–size scaling relationships according to different invertebrate phylogenetic groups from published literature. Soil invertebrate collection from all other geographic regions followed similar procedures, whereby mesofauna were collected either from small cores (5 cm diameter, 10 cm deep) or 16×16 cm quadrats (5 cm deep), and macrofauna were collected from large soil cores (20 cm diameter, 10 cm deep), leaf litter sieving (0.5 m2 ECOWORM and 1 m2 EFFForTS), and mustard extraction for earthworms (0.25 m2). Invertebrate body size ranged from 4.82×10–5 mg – 5290 mg. For more detailed methods see Antunes.

To analyse size–energy use relationships, we took a size–binning (rather than populations of competing organisms) approach by taking the natural logarithm of all body sizes, across all taxonomic groups, and grouped them into 0.25 ln(mg) size class bins (following Reuman). This size binning approach was used for two reasons. Firstly, population-level information (i.e., species level taxonomic resolution) was not always available for our data, though individual body sizes were. Secondly, these methods have both yielded similar size–density scaling relationships within many food webs studied, so we can assume this consistency also applies to tests of size–energy use scaling relationships. We took the median of the natural logarithm of body size of each size class bin per plot, across all taxonomic groups. Abundance was then calculated as the number of individuals in each size class bin (and per node type for analysing within trophic levels) per plot and scaled to 1 m2. For analysing size–density relationships, the counts of soil invertebrate fresh body sizes (mg) across and within trophic levels were scaled up to 1 m2. We calculated individual metabolic rates I (J hr–1) for invertebrates within each taxonomic group (see Table S3 for regressions applied to each taxon) using the following equation from Ehnes et al.

I=exp(ln(io)+α×ln(M)−E/(k×T)) (1)

Where k is Boltzmann’s constant (8.62×10–5), T is environmental temperature in Kelvin, E the activation energy, io the taxa specific normalisation constant and, α is the allometric exponent. Plot–level mean soil temperature from a three–month period preceding soil sampling was collected using data loggers for the Aotearoa New Zealand. Local area–level annual soil temperature (over a one year period) for the ECOWORM plots was collected from online weather databases (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration n.d.). Plot–level mean soil temperature was collected over a 2.5 month period using data loggers for the EFFForTS data. We took the natural logarithm of individual invertebrate metabolic rates, summed per size class bin per plot, and scaled to 1 m2.

Foodwebreconstructionandconsumerenergyintakecalculation
To reconstruct soil food webs, nodes were defined according to organism taxonomic order (or family level for Hymenoptera and Coleoptera) for which information on their general feeding preferences was obtained. We constructed a meta–matrix of binary consumer–resource interactions, where feeding links were assigned based on feeding preferences obtained from literature. Energy influx in J day–1 into each consumer node within a local food web (i.e., plot) was calculated using the food–web energetics approach as described by Barnes and Gauzens to quantify the energy intake of organisms across the 183 local food webs. To calculate energy fluxes, we assumed that losses in energy from consumer nodes (via metabolism and predation) were balanced by intake of energy through resource consumption. Energy flux values were calculated taking into account the assimilation efficiency of energy by consumers based on the resources they feed on (i.e., primary versus secondary consumers).

Using the fluxing function from the fluxweb package in R, the influx of energy to consumer (j) was calculated as:

Σi(Wij×eij×Fij)=Ij+Σj(Wij×Fj) (2)

where eij is the assimilation efficiency by which a consumer (j) converts energy consumed from its resource (i) into energy for metabolism and biomass production. To determine the assimilation efficiency of energy by consumers based on the resources they feed on, eij was set to 0.906 for animals (e.g., as resources of predators), 0.545 for plants, 0.158 for detritus, 0.6 for bacteria, and 0.5 for fungi. Metabolic rate Ij for all animal consumers was equal to the summed individual metabolic rates per node, per plot. Ij was set to 1 for all basal resources (bacteria, detritus, plants, and fungi). Fij=Wij×Fj is the flux of energy to a consumer where Fj is the sum of fluxes into a node and Wij is the proportion of Fj obtained by the node according to scaled consumer preferences (wij) to the biomasses of different available prey as:

Wij=wij×Bi / Σj×wij×Bj (3)

where Bi and Bj are the resource and consumer biomasses, respectively. Bi for all animal resources and Bj for all animal consumers were equal to the summed fresh body masses (mg) of all individuals per node type, per plot. All basal resource biomasses were set to be equal to the average biomass of all consumer node types per plot to set near–equal preferences of omnivores between predatory links and basal resources. This was done to reduce extreme preferences of omnivores towards basal resources, such as plants and detritus that typically have much higher biomasses compared to soil invertebrate prey, but are less preferred by them as they are lower in nutritional value. Studies have tested whether the assignment of feeding preferences of omnivores between basal resources (in this case, just plants) and animals could affect energy fluxes by altering feeding preferences for plants between 0.2 to 0.9 and found no significant change in the outcome of their analysis; therefore, we set equal preferences between basal resources and animal prey in our food webs. Additionally, to reduce the amount of energy predators consume from their own biomass pool and unrealistic feeding preferences toward cannibalism, we set the feeding preferences of any cannibalistic links to 0.1.

Because body size was grouped into size class bins (irrespective of food web node) per plot to analyse size–energy relationships and energy flux was calculated per food web node per plot (Fnode), to attribute the proportion of ingoing energy flux from each food web node to each size class bin per plot (Fsizeclass), we calculated proportional energy flux according to the summed metabolism of each size class (Isizeclass) and energy intake of that node as:

Fsizeclass= f(Isizeclass,node =Inode)×Fnode (4)

Where Inode represents the total metabolism of a node. Energy fluxes were then natural logarithm–transformed and scaled to 1 m2.

To obtain food web metrics that could explain variation in expectations of size–density scaling and energetic equivalence of soil food webs, we quantified mean trophic similarity among nodes (for the whole food web, and within primary and secondary consumers) by calculating the average Jaccard similarity among consumer nodes based on their feeding links with resource nodes. Specifically, trophic similarity TSij between consumer i and j represents the similarity in their diets, estimated with a Jaccard index:

TSij=|Pi∩Pj|/|Pi∪Pj| (5)

Pi represents the set of prey of consumer i and |Pi ∩ Pj| is the cardinality of the intersection of Pi and Pj (i.e., the number of prey common to consumer i and j). High trophic similarity indicates a large average overlap among consumers, which can occur in the absence of omnivory, e.g. if many specialists feed on a shared resource. We calculated observed node richness as the number of nodes within each food web (total nodes in the food web, and the number of primary and secondary consumer nodes). Furthermore, we calculated trophic level omnivory of secondary consumer i (Oi) as the variance of the trophic levels of its prey:

Oi=1/ni Σj=1...ni(TLj−TLx̄i)2 (6)

Where TLx̄i is the average trophic level of the prey of species i. For each local food web, we further determined the prey–averaged trophic level (TLi) of each node, such that the trophic level was equal to one for basal resources, two for primary consumers, and >2 for secondary consumers as:

TLi=1/ni Σj=1...niTLj (7)

Where ni is the number of prey of species i, and j are prey of species i.

Statisticalanalysis
To analyse size–density relationships (N∝Mb) across whole soil invertebrate food webs and within primary and secondary consumers, we used maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to estimate the exponent b (i.e., λ+1) derived from individual size distributions (ISD) of all individual body sizes (scaled to 1 m2) within soil invertebrate communities using the sizeSpectra package in R. To check the fit of models against observed body size data (x), rank–frequency plots were produced giving the natural logarithm–rank of the number of observations ≥x against the value of x.

To analyse size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn), and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn) scaling relationships across whole soil invertebrate food webs and within primary and secondary consumers, we used ordinary least squared (OLS) regression using logarithm median body mass data (scaled to 1 m2). MLE and OLS regression models were run across all communities (i.e., plots) within the four geographic regions. The 95% confidence intervals around the exponent values were also calculated, and exponents were considered to meet N∝M–0.75, In ∝ Mn 0, or Fn ∝ Mn 0 expectations if these confidence intervals included the expected exponent value. We excluded all resulting models with less than 10 body size class bins or individuals per food web from our analysis due to insufficient data for estimating reliable model fits. To evaluate the distribution of scaling exponents around the mean and median values of our models, we calculated the kurtosis of their probability density functions using the kurtosis function in R. In this regard, higher kurtosis values indicate greater deviation from a normal distribution, reflecting increased variation around the mean and median exponent values. We also ran a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, to determine if our two sample distributions (e.g., metabolism and energy flux exponents) come from the same probability distribution using the ks.test function in R. To analyse size–metabolism (In ∝ Mn), and size–energy flux (Fn ∝ Mn) scaling relationships across whole soil invertebrate food webs and within primary and secondary consumers, we also used ranged major axis (RMA) regression using the lmodel2 package in R to analyse these relationships. RMA regression is used when both x and y variables (e.g., median body size, abundance, metabolism, and energy flux) in the regression equation are random. RMA regression models were run across all communities (i.e., plots) within the four geographic regions. We excluded all resulting models with less than 10 body size class bins or individuals per food web from our analysis due to insufficient data for estimating reliable model fits. As a result, our analyses yielded a total of 183 food webs (i.e., comprising both primary and secondary consumers) and 360 trophic level models (180 models for primary consumers and 180 for secondary consumer food webs). Our analyses yielded a total of 183 food webs (i.e., comprising both primary and secondary consumers) and 355 trophic level models (173 models for primary consumers and 179 for secondary consumer food webs).

Additionally, we investigated whether the likelihood of size–density and size–energy use relationships to meet EER expectations could be explained by variation in food web structure. To do so, for all food webs, we constructed a normal linear model testing for the response of the absolute logarithm–deviation of observed exponents from expected size–energy use exponents (In ∝ Mn 0 and Fn ∝ Mn 0) to omnivory, node richness, and trophic similarity per food web and per trophic level (i.e., primary and secondary consumers). This produced six linear models in total. All statistical analyses were performed in R version R 4.4.0.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This paper focuses on the Energy Equivalence Rule (EER) that predicts that population energy use is invariant with average body-size. The authors have examined the EER by applying it on a large dataset including 183 soil food webs across the globe, taking into consideration the trophic position of the species under study.
The strengths of the study are:
1. The validity of the EER is a timely question and is subject of debate from theoretical as well as empirical perspectives.
2. The dataset used is unique given the number of food webs and species under study, as well as the global distribution of the food webs. The food webs are nicely comparable as they are all soil food webs.
3. The study is scientifically novel, as the application of the EER on the dataset takes into consideration aspects of food web architecture and the trophic positioning of the species.
4. Also novel is de comparison between measures of population metabolism and total energy flux.
5. The study is well carried out.
6. The results are well presented with an adequate number of clarifying figures.
7. The results are scientifically interesting and relevant, as the soil food webs seem to deviate from the EER in a principal and statistically significant manner. Expectations regarding trophic positioning (primary, secondary, predatory consumers) seem to be confirmed, although not always at the level of statistical significance.
8. The findings are well discussed but see my remarks below.
On the basis of these strengths the study qualifies to be published in a high quality scientific journal.
But I have the following concerns regarding the present manuscript.
1. The introduction could have been clearer regarding the state-of-the-art in this field of research. Then it becomes also clearer what the novelty of the study is and how it stands out from other studies. An important piece of novelty is the consideration of aspects of food web architecture and the trophic position of the species. In the manuscript lines 132 -134 states that variation in food web architecture is unexplored, but this statement should be made more explicit. There is a number of studies in which the EER is applied to datasets including food webs. In one of these studies a large number of soil food webs is analysed (ref 20). And in another study (ref. 1) categories of species are distinguished in part based on their trophic position. It would be helpful when the present study is contrasted to such studies. For example, in terms of what they did and found rather than only mentioning that they have been done.
In this context I like to mention a study not referred to in the present manuscript, i.e. Evolution of body size in food webs: does the energetic equivalence rule hold? by Nicolas Loeuille and Michel Loreau in Ecology Letters, (2006) 9: 171–178. In this study the authors model how food web structure evolves from body-size and ecological interactions. The study might be relevant for sharpening the research question.
2. I am a little uncertain whether I fully understood the results, but what I see is that the soil food webs deviate very strongly from the EER. The size-density index is found to be -0.174 instead of -0.75 (correct?). This is a lot. If the indexes for size-population metabolism and the size-energy flux are 0.134 and 0.204 respectively, then the index for individual size-metabolism should be around 0.5, i.e. smaller than 0.75, but less deviating than the index for size-density. I would emphasize this finding more. This makes the paper more challenging as to me the soil food webs do confirm the EER (at all).
3. I miss a discussion of how the present results relate to the findings for the soil food webs examined in ref. 20. Also, a comparison with the results given in ref 1. seems relevant.
4. The results that discriminate between types of consumers are interesting, make sense, and are discussed well. But they might also be viewed in the context of the deviating values for the food webs as a whole.
5. EER is seen as a rule, but it can also be seen as a hypothesis. The present study formulates hypotheses regarding trophic position, competition and ways to quantify population energy use, so we have hypotheses on top of the EER hypothesis, which makes it sometimes difficult to see what ‘expectations’ mean.
6. The conclusion drawn in lines 364-368 I find too mild. I don’t think that deviations from the EER is the most promising way to understand population dynamics in soil ecosystems. In the discussion numerous factors and processes are mentioned that influence these dynamics in fundamental ways. And soil populations are known for their large variation in numbers among soils and within soils over time and space. Isn’t it possible to simply reject the EER for soil food webs. We then should not throw away the baby with the washing water of course. The rejection comes from the assumed relationship between body-size and abundance, which to me is the weaker part of the EER (see also ref. 25 and Isaac et al. Global Ecology and Biogeography, 2013, 22, 1–5). The relationship between body-size and individual metabolism though is well based on biological/physiological arguments and has proven to be of value for understanding food web structure and also the structure of soil food webs.
Hope my comments are helpful in making the positioning of the study somewhat clearer and the implications of the findings somewhat more pronounced.

5. L 139-140: Using energy input (consumption) before assimilation may be an
unreliable method of estimating population energy use, especially if assimilation
efficiency is low and variable. Note that assimilation efficiency tends to be much
higher for animal (secondary) versus plant (primary) consumers. Please clarify.
Reponse: We took much care in accounting for assimilation efficiency in energy
intake calculations. Please see section “Food web reconstruction and consumer
energy flux calculation” within the supplementary information. Energy intake before
assimilation quantifies total resource consumption, taking into account the different
energetic demands of consumers due to different assimilation efficiencies of
organisms at different trophic levels. If we were to rather use energy intake after
assimilation, this would not account for the proportionately greater consumption rates
of lower trophic level organisms (e.g. detritivores) needed to balance their energetic
demands, as compared to predators that have relatively high assimilation
efficiencies. Therefore, we calculate energy intake per population by scaling
consumption rates according to varying assimilation efficiencies among trophic
levels. This is necessary because energetic equivalence will depend on competition
among consumers for resources based on total rates of exploitation of those
resources, rather than the proportion of energy that is eventually assimilated by
consumers.
